en: If this son survives,
They will say he shall overthrow the Oirats.
As a famed gray-wolf hero,
His renown will spread throughout the world.
Akun Khan, khan of Afghanistan—
His daughter Aichürök
Will become the wife he takes.
In my dream I caught a charger:
Its shoes were fine and its tether golden,
And I tied it fast and secure.
This one became a star in the heavens,
The eternal companion
Of my son in the next world,
The finest of women.
The luckless peri-born maiden,
The daughter of wealthy Kaiypchal,
Is the strength of your noble hero,
The lioness among women.
If your son meets hardship,
She is the one who will deliver him
From his cruel and grievous enemy.’
So spoke the dervish,
Giving his blessing to my undertaking
And revealing a sign in my dream.
Kuyaly, daughter of Kaiypchal,
Is the finest of women,
A daughter born of light.
She bears the name of woman,
But for her womanhood
She would be a renowned champion of the world.
Her courage is extraordinary,
Her strength beyond measure;
Her nature is unlike any other’s,
A peerless, noble-browed champion.
That maiden is a lionhearted hero,
Shielded by the unseen spirits.
In the end she will be found
As a bride for your son.
By destiny she will come to you
And become your son’s inheritance.
She is the blessing of the Night of Destiny;
She will rekindle your extinguished fire
And save your soul from death.
Joining much that has been severed,
Firmly gathering what was scattered,
She is the one who will gladden your heart.
She will increase your laughter;
She is the black fortress-city,
The priceless treasure beyond finding.
From the hidden arrow of death,
From the accursed missile of hell,
From the grip of terrible calamity,
From the iron snare that entangles,
From the mighty arm and potent venom
Of the savage dog,
From the maw of the devourer of nations,
From the black gaze of the monster—
She is the hero who will deliver him.
Listen well, Kanykei,
To the words I spoke long ago:
The peri-born Kuyaly
Is herself another noble hero.
She will become your daughter-in-law,
And her word will be honored by the people.
If you so desire, the Night of Destiny will come;
She is the steadfast strength behind you.
She is the soul who will await
The blessed one who restores your power.
If Kuyaly comes to you,
She will enrich the crown of your yurt.
She will make your true gray-wolf son
Khan over lands in every direction.
She will gild the lattice walls of your yurt;
When your son comes of age,
She will make him a mighty khan like Katar.
Though the high, imposing coat stands ready,
When she comes, she will water his horse.
While ears can hear and eyes can see,
She will spread his fame among the people.
She is the blessing of the Night of Destiny,
A heavenly maiden created by God,
The one who will bring joy to the soul.
If your daughter-in-law Kuyaly remains well,
She will fulfill your heart’s desire.
The small, dark leather purses
She will fill with much gold,
Fulfilling all your wishes.
The heavy saddlebags and leather sacks
She will fill with goods of yellow gold.
Her heart will bring peace to the people;
Destroying many enemies,
You will see her become the foremost khan.
When your daughter-in-law Kuyaly comes,
A charger will be tied at your hitching rail,
And broad cauldrons will boil.
You will prosper in abundance
And flourish like luxuriant grass.
She is the one you must await,
The soul who will care for your hearth.
When she becomes your daughter-in-law,
Your charger will come to your throne,
And your falcon will be ready for training.
Your champion will bear a quiver,
And your stature will be like Mount Kap.
Will any mortal dare confront you?
Will an enemy dare attack head-on?
Will he covetously attempt
To strike from a cold mountain pass?
Will he cross the Barmak Mountains
And come striding bare-legged?
Your daughter-in-law a champion, your son a lion—
Can any threatening foe defeat them?
Her prowess is extraordinary,
Her days of glory will be many;
She is the generous bringer of good fortune,
The soul you must await,
The very embodiment of true prosperity,
The dark eye of blessed destiny.
When Kuyaly becomes your daughter-in-law,
You, fierce and imposing woman,
Will be the Night of Destiny to the city.
Sacred as mighty Mount Kap,
You will be a saint incarnate.
Consider and understand what I say;
Through the words I have spoken truly,
Good fortune will come to you.
Its collar will be fine and its tether golden;
A true falcon will alight upon your hand.
If it survives, the noble one
Will become entangled in your golden net
And one day fall into your hands.
Peerless will be your steed,
And your kinsmen will camp beside you.
Your enemies will leave your thoughts;
They will cling together like curds and befriend you,
Those enemies with whom you once shed blood,
And your wish will fall into your hands.’
So spoke the dervish,
Taking my hand and drawing me close.
While I lay sleeping in my dream,
He startled me with a sudden shove.
My snoring stopped,
And my eyes flew wide as scattered flour.
I swiftly awoke from my dream,
My heart pounding like a horse,
For I had received tidings from the unseen.
My dear heart rejoiced,
And I wondered where the famed champion Kuyaly
Had been born,
And in what land her mother
Had given birth to that champion.
He could traverse a horse’s whole course;
Across the entire wide world,
He could roam in twelve days.
He knew seventy different tongues
And traveled freely over the earth.
So to Agybai, son of the Argyn khan,
The interpreter of that gray wolf,
I gave six swift horses
And a letter small as my palm,
Dressed him in a fine gray robe,
And mounted him on the swift camel.
To discover whether she was indeed
The destined bride of the noble lion
And return with certain knowledge,
I mounted him on the swift camel
And sent him journeying across the earth,
Quenching his thirst with sunshine,
Feeding him provisions rich as külaзык,
And clothing him in flowered silk,
While the mount grew stronger with each day’s ride.
Mounting him on the swift camel,
I sent Agybai on his way.
Without letting a single soul know,
Without giving any person an inkling,
Without the gossipers learning of it,
Without even the dust-bearing wind knowing,
I spread out abundant wealth and countless livestock—
Pure gold coins and precious stones—
Before Agybai,
Saying, “Take these as gifts.”
Displaying all my riches,
I made poor Agybai,
From that time until this,
Grasp the holy Quran.
I had him pierce a steel bullet,
Chew a loaf of gray-wheat bread,
And swear ninety varied and solemn oaths
That he would reveal nothing.
I made him lick the sword’s edge
And swear upon immediate death.
“My dear Agybai,
When you mount Endik, rein in his mouth;
Among witless people, restrain your tongue.
The sorrowful words I have spoken
Have a name heard, but no visible form.
Kuyaly, daughter of Kaiypchal,
Is destined to be my daughter-in-law,
My daughter-in-law for the world hereafter,
The dark eye of prosperity.
My son Semetey,
A lion surpassing all heroes,
Is the one she shall marry.
She is the Night of Destiny itself.
My dear Agybai,
Learn where the champion Kuyaly
Sows her grain;
Learn her lineage, worthy of a father,
And the land where her clan took root.
If you return knowing this, Agybai,
We shall arrange the match while we live:
Setting aside many thousands of mares,
Separating double-humped camels,
And allotting abundant wealth and livestock,
With a white kerchief bound upon the brow,
We shall drive all the livestock
To seal the marriage pact.
Let us place a halter around her neck
And fetters upon her feet;
Let us hold a feast beneath the open sky
And take that proud one
To be our daughter-in-law.
Bringing her into the white palace,
We shall serve abundant kinds of sweet food.
Made Ajybay drink,
Dressed him in Jekeyboz,
And mounted Ajybay
On the dark swift camel that flew like a cloud,
Outstripping the wind,
For I had conceived a wondrous plan,
And was carrying out that wonder.
To poor Ajybay
I commanded, “Find the warrior maiden,”
Thus giving him my order.
“Range across the breadth of the earth,
Traverse the whole world,
Reach and explore it all.
Through the world’s four corners
Travel everywhere,
And of all the created earth
Leave not one place unsearched.
Visit the five corners of the known world,
Circle them five times,
And discover the known abode
Of that valiant, ill-fated maiden.
If by chance you return without seeing her,
Then may you behold the land of no return,
And cease to walk among the living.
If you are truly a formidable man,
If you, Ajybay, are a lion,
Discover the ancestry
And lineage of that hapless one.
If you will not go and search the earth,
If you ignore your sister-in-law’s courteous words
And fail to find the warrior maiden,
Your words will become mere boasting;
